title: Make a Research and Discovery Plan
editorial_note: Automated dialogue draft from the revised lesson. Review spoken wording and meaning before publishing.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Today we're talking about Make a Research and Discovery Plan. By the end, you'll know why this matters, how to use it, and what to notice in a real product.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What is the problem we are trying to understand?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A discovery plan is a route from uncertainty to action. Begin with decisions and their dates:

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at plan backward from decisions?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: choose or revise the problem frame; select among intervention families; include or exclude a population, channel, or use; commit to data, policy, service, or technical architecture; prototype, pilot, expand, pause, or stop; accept, mitigate, or escalate risk.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: For each decision, identify owner, contributors, consequence if wrong, assumptions, existing evidence, remaining uncertainty, evidence threshold, and likely response. If no plausible result can change the decision, the activity is not decision research. It may be monitoring, stakeholder engagement, or documentation—and should be named honestly.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at turn assumptions into research questions?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Avoid vague goals such as “understand clinic choice.” Ask questions tied to a mechanism:

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: How do patients currently distinguish eligibility, service facts, inference, and promotion? Which clinic facts actually change choice or produce recovery when wrong? How are those facts created, owned, updated, and contested? What happens under proxy, non-digital, assistive-technology, and low-capacity clinic conditions?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Which source-state presentation supports appropriate confidence and action? Can proposed owners complete verification under realistic workload? What outcome and guardrail pattern would justify a bounded pilot?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Separate exploratory, descriptive, evaluative, causal, and monitoring questions. Each needs different evidence.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at match method to claim?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use methods for what they can establish:

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Interviews: meaning, past episodes, expectations, language, consequence, and reported behaviour. Contextual inquiry/observation: actual work, tacit judgement, interruption, tools, workarounds, and environment. Diary or longitudinal study: events and change that are difficult to observe directly.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Content/data audit: source quality, duplication, missingness, lifecycle, and structure. Journey or service mapping: actors, handoffs, waits, ownership, and systemic opportunity. Concept testing: comprehension and perceived relevance of alternative value propositions.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Usability/accessibility evaluation: task performance, understanding, error, recovery, and inclusive operation under tested conditions. Technical spike/simulation: integration, latency, data, reliability, and operational feasibility. Survey: distribution of clearly defined attitudes or self-reports in a defensible sample.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Experiment: comparative causal effect under explicit assignment, exposure, measures, and assumptions. Telemetry/analytics: recorded behaviour and distribution, interpreted with instrumentation and selection limits.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Triangulate when one method cannot support the decision. Do not collect multiple weak signals merely to say methods were mixed.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Design the sample around relevant variation
turns.text: What changes when we look at design the sample around relevant variation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: “Users” are not one participant group. Recruit conditions that can change the mechanism:

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: first versus repeat referral; access or scheduling need; digital versus supported/non-digital route; self versus proxy action; language and literacy context; clinic size, governance capacity, region, and integration maturity; coordinator expertise and workload; successful, failed, corrected, and abandoned cases.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Sampling is a claim boundary. A small qualitative sample can expose mechanisms and severe problems; it does not estimate population prevalence. Purposefully include rare high-consequence cases rather than allowing traffic frequency to define importance.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Build ethics and operations into the plan
turns.text: What changes when we look at build ethics and operations into the plan?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Specify recruitment access, informed consent, sensitive topics, participant support, withdrawal, recording, storage, retention, tool/vendor use, anonymisation limits, and compensation. Plan accommodations and alternate participation; do not exclude people because the research setup is inaccessible.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Account for recruitment lead time, clinic permission, staff workload, researcher capacity, prototype readiness, instrumentation, and analysis. Protect time for complete-case reading, contradiction, and peer review. Fast research is credible when scope and claims are bounded, not when analysis is removed.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Define disconfirming evidence and stopping rules
turns.text: What changes when we look at define disconfirming evidence and stopping rules?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Write what would weaken the frame or concept:

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Predetermine revise, narrow, escalate, or stop responses. This prevents research from becoming an elaborate confirmation ritual.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Synthesis is part of the plan
turns.text: What changes when we look at synthesis is part of the plan?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Define how observations become claims: recordings and notes, evidence units, coding or structured comparison, counterexamples, analyst memos, confidence, and decision brief. Preserve observation → interpretation → implication → recommendation.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Share emerging evidence with limitations while it can still alter work. The final output should state supported and prohibited claims, not just themes. Store reusable evidence with consent and provenance; a repository is not useful if later teams cannot judge method and context.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: payment failure?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A team has two weeks to choose between clearer error content, retry changes, and alternate payment. The plan combines funnel/error telemetry, support-case review, observation of failed tasks, provider technical investigation, and prototype recovery testing. Each evidence stream answers a different decision.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Generic interviews about checkout satisfaction would not locate the mechanism.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at where this can go wrong?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Method calendar: activities are scheduled without a decision they can change. Question–claim mismatch: interviews estimate prevalence or analytics claim motivation. Recruitment convenience: easy participants exclude the context where consequence is highest. Happy-path stimulus: prototypes omit uncertainty, policy, latency, and recovery.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Confirmation architecture: only supporting results have a defined response. Ethics as paperwork: consent exists while data reuse, distress, or exclusion remains unmanaged. Report endpoint: findings have an audience but no owner, threshold, or next action. Analysis compression: speed is achieved by removing contradiction and contextual judgement.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Senior researchers protect decision quality under constraint. They narrow claims before weakening method, make organisational feasibility a research question, and refuse activities whose result cannot influence a choice. They negotiate timing so evidence arrives before irreversible commitment and ensure high-consequence minority contexts are not averaged away.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: <! -- Editorial: manual revision; curated product example --

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Illustrative scenario: a clinic scheduling service. A team must decide whether to build self-service rescheduling. Its plan names the decision owner and deadline, observes current work, interviews people who abandoned the flow, checks staff capacity, and tests a simple alternative. Each method is chosen for the uncertainty it can reduce while the decision is still changeable.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Read a research plan and underline every method. For each, locate the decision, claim, participant boundary, evidence threshold, and response. If you cannot, rewrite one activity from “conduct interviews” into a question whose possible answers lead to different actions.
